title: Comparison of entangling strategies for unitary synthesis
authors: Jonas Wunder, Hendrik Weimer, Ricardo Costa de Almeida
abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers are promising as a platform for realizing quantum computational advantage. They promise long coherence times, near all-to-all connectivity, and potential multiqubit gates as distinguishing advantages compared to competing platforms. Regarding these advantages, it is crucial to understand the trade-offs between increasing engineering complexity and actual improvements in running quantum algorithms with a more flexible gate set. In this work, we investigate this question and develop a versatile toolset to evaluate the performance of gate sets composed of native Mølmer--Sørensen multiqubit gates. To this end, we employ unitary synthesis as an application-agnostic benchmark target and identify specific hardware requirements for multiqubit gates to be advantageous.
summary: This work analyzes which entangling gate set is best suited for quantum computation on trapped-ion platforms by benchmarking unitary synthesis. By varying the complexity of the gate set and modeling hardware error scaling, the authors determine that the optimal strategy is highly dependent on the underlying physical error model. This provides crucial guidance for hardware engineers designing scalable quantum processors.
main_problem: The paper investigates the trade-off between increasing the engineering complexity of a gate set (e.g., using more complex multiqubit gates) and the actual performance gain when synthesizing arbitrary quantum unitaries.
main_result: The optimal entangling strategy depends critically on the assumed scaling of hardware gate errors: full-register gates are superior under linear error scaling, while two-qubit gates can dominate under quadratic error scaling.
method: The authors developed a versatile toolset using variational quantum circuits (ansatz) to benchmark unitary synthesis against Haar-random target unitaries.
model_or_system: The study focuses on trapped-ion quantum computers, utilizing native Mølmer–Sørensen (MS) multiqubit gates alongside single-qubit rotations to construct the quantum circuit ansatz.
key_observables: Gate fidelity ($F$), infidelity ($1-F$), total circuit depth, and the number of entangling gates used.
important_parameters: The scaling exponent of gate infidelity (linear $N_g$ vs. quadratic $N_g^2$) and the number of qubits ($N=4, 6$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that gates within a single entangling layer can run in parallel, and the comparison is benchmarked against synthesizing Haar-random unitaries.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of the variational ansatz for different entangling strategies (e.g., 4a vs. 22a22b22c). Performance plots show fidelity vs. circuit depth, demonstrating how the optimal strategy changes based on the assumed error scaling.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of gate set comparison, develops the general variational ansatz, benchmarks performance using unitary synthesis, and finally analyzes the results by comparing strategies under different error scaling models.
why_interesting: It provides quantitative, hardware-aware guidelines for quantum algorithm design, directly informing which physical gate set (e.g., all-to-all vs. nearest-neighbor) is most resource-efficient for a given error model.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two examples of variational quantum circuits with periodic ansatz as in Equations (2) and (4). The circuit on the left is the basic ansatz for four qubits, corresponding to strategy 4a, consisting of single qubit rotations about the z- and x-axis followed by a collective MS gate. On the right, we have entangling strategy 4a22a which employs a pair of two-qubit MS gates every second entangling pulse when compared to 4a. Parametric dependencies are omitted for brevity.

Figure 2: Infidelities of different entangling strategies when synthesizing random four-qubit unitaries at different circuit depths. For illustrative purposes, three differ- ent x-axis transformations are shown. Data points show the average fidelity achieved out of 500 different target unitaries. On the left, the x-axis is simply the number of layers of the circuit. The middle plot contain the same data but with the total gate count as the x-axis, equally counting entangling gates and single qubit rotations. On the right, only entangling gates are counted on the x-axis.

Figure 3: Optimality rate of different entangling strategies at different circuit depths. Optimality rate is defined as the relative number of target unitaries for which the respective entangling strategy produces the highest fidelity. Strategies color coded as in Figure 2.

Figure 4: Infidelities of different entangling strategies when synthesizing random six-qubit unitaries at different circuit depths. Data points show the average fidelity achieved out of 100 different target unitaries. We observe similar features as in Fig- ure 4. However, the right panel shows entangling strategies with the same number of parameters per entangling layer, and a one can observe deviations among them for large layer count, unlike for the four-qubit strategies.

Figure 5: Optimal infidelities for strategy 4a when accounting for hardware infideli- ties. On the left, results for good entangling with all idling regimes, worst idling in lighter shades. Similarly, on the right, we show results for bad entangling.
